A_target.statement:
Let $V$ be a [[Definition:Vector Space|vector space]] over $\C$ with $1 \le \dim V < \infty$.
Let $T: V \to V$ be a [[Definition:Linear Operator|linear operator]].
Then there exist $\mathbf v \ne \mathbf 0$ and $\lambda \in \C$ such that:
:$T \mathbf v = \lambda \mathbf v$

B_source.statement:
Let $T$ be an [[Definition:Invertible Linear Transformation|invertible]] linear operator on $V$.
Then the induced [[Definition:Holomorphic Function|holomorphic]] map on the [[Definition:Projective Space|projective space]] $\map {\Bbb P} V$ has a [[Definition:Fixed Point|fixed point]].

substitutions.the linear map T: the induced map on lines through the origin

object_map.reformulation: The eigenvector equation is only defined up to scaling, so it must be moved to the projective quotient where it becomes a genuine fixed-point statement.

validity_conditions: T must be invertible for the induced map on projective space to be everywhere defined; the singular case is handled separately since zero is then an eigenvalue
the field must be algebraically closed for the fixed point to exist, which is where complexity is used
the vector space must be finite-dimensional so projective space is compact
proof_plan: Pass from $V$ to the [[Definition:Projective Space|projective space]] $\map {\Bbb P} V$ of lines through $\mathbf 0$.

A [[Definition:Linear Operator|linear operator]] sends lines to lines.
If $T$ is not invertible, any $\mathbf v \in \map \ker T \setminus \set {\mathbf 0}$ is an eigenvector with $\lambda = 0$.
Otherwise $T$ induces a self-map $\bar T$ of $\map {\Bbb P} V$.
A fixed point $\sqbrk {\mathbf v}$ of $\bar T$ is precisely a $T$-[[Definition:Invariant Subspace|invariant]] one-dimensional subspace $\C \mathbf v$.
By the source result, over $\C$, $\bar T$ has a fixed point $\sqbrk {\mathbf v}$.

Then $T \mathbf v \in \C \mathbf v$, so $T \mathbf v = \lambda \mathbf v$ for some $\lambda \in \C$, which is the [[Definition:Eigenvalue of Linear Operator|eigenvalue]].
{{qed}}
